analysis.one_liner: Strips EPA authority to regulate greenhouse gases and voids major federal climate rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 122 House Republicans, never got a vote and died in committee when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the Clean Air Act so that carbon dioxide, methane, and other greenhouse gases are not "air pollutants" the EPA can regulate, and it declares that no federal law authorizes regulating climate change. It would also void two finished EPA rules — one limiting methane leaks from new oil and gas wells, and the Clean Power Plan limiting carbon from power plants. Finally, it would bar any EPA rule that could cost jobs from taking effect unless Congress and the President approved it.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas producers, coal companies, and utilities with fossil-fired power plants. The bill would void the methane rule covering their new wells and the Clean Power Plan's carbon limits on their power plants, and would permanently remove greenhouse gases from every major environmental law, preventing any future administration from reinstating federal climate rules.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Clean Air Act so carbon dioxide, methane, water vapor, and other greenhouse gases are excluded from the definition of 'air pollutant,' and declares that no federal law authorizes or requires regulating climate change — ending the legal basis for federal climate rules.

Voids two completed EPA rules outright: the 2016 methane emission standards for new oil and gas sources, and the 2015 carbon pollution rules for existing power plants (the Clean Power Plan), nullifying them 'and any similar or successor rules.'

Requires the EPA to analyze the gross and net employment impact of every proposed rule, and forbids any rule with a negative employment impact from taking effect unless Congress approves it and the President signs it.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people, through dirtier air, unchecked methane and carbon pollution from power plants and oil and gas operations, and the accelerating costs of climate change. The employment veto would also make any air-quality or water-quality rule that costs even a few jobs vulnerable to congressional blockage.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, via dirtier air and climate damages

drawbacks.text: The bill would eliminate the federal government's main legal tools for limiting climate pollution, by removing greenhouse gases from the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and other statutes, with no replacement program for limiting carbon or methane emissions.

The employment provision is far broader than climate policy: it would apply to every EPA rule, so any regulation — including standards on toxic air, water pollution, or waste — could be blocked indefinitely whenever an employment analysis predicted job losses, giving Congress a veto over routine public-health protection.

Supporters' strongest argument is a real one: the EPA rules at issue were projected to accelerate coal plant and oilfield closures, costing jobs in coal and oil- and gas-producing regions, and the bill's findings argue that Congress, not a federal agency, should decide whether to regulate greenhouse gases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real protection for fossil-fuel workers whose jobs the targeted rules threatened, and its claim that Congress should set climate policy rather than an agency is a legitimate constitutional position. But the cost is one-sided: it would erase, with no replacement, the country's principal legal authority to limit the pollution driving climate change, and its jobs provision would hamstring EPA protection of air and water generally, not just climate rules. The costs fall broadly on the public; the savings accrue to a specific set of polluting industries.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees the day it was introduced, no committee ever acted on it, and it died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Gary Palmer introduced the bill on January 24, 2017, with 96 original cosponsors, the day after President Trump's inauguration.

It was referred to four committees — Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Agriculture — and then to the Water Resources and Environment subcommittee the next day.
It gathered 122 cosponsors, all Republicans, but no committee held a markup or vote and the House never considered it; the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal interests lost their chance at permanent statutory immunity from federal climate rules, but nothing changed in practice because the bill never advanced. The public kept the Clean Air Act's authority over greenhouse gases on the books, though the bill's death created no new protections either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public, by default, as the bill died

for.name: Rep. Gary Palmer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 96 original cosponsors on introduction day.

for.name: 122 of 241 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it majority support among House Republicans but no path to a floor vote.

against.name: Chairmen of the four committees of referral (Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, Transportation and Infrastructure, Agriculture)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out; no hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: All 122 cosponsors were Republicans — none of the chamber's 194 Democrats signed on — and the bill never reached a vote, so no formal roll call exists.

industries.note: The bill would void the EPA's 2016 methane emission standards for new and modified oil and gas sources and bar any successor rule, eliminating a compliance cost the industry had fought. The savings would come at the expense of nearby residents breathing the emissions.

industries.industry: Coal mining and coal-fired electric utilities
industries.note: The bill would void the Clean Power Plan's carbon limits on existing power plants and declare that no law regulates climate change, lifting the main federal constraint on coal generation. Coal-producing regions would keep jobs longer, while the public bears the carbon pollution.

By removing greenhouse gases from the Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, and waste laws, the bill would shield all industrial emitters from climate-related permitting and regulation, and the blanket employment test would slow other EPA rules that affect them.
